summary: Adds examples of how to identify IPv6 and MPLS protocols in the Remote Network Monitoring (RMON) MIB's protocol directory. It extends the identifier examples given in RFC 2896 so monitoring tools can describe these newer protocols.

plainLanguage.summary: A bird-watching guide needs a name tag for each bird. This memo adds name tags for two newer kinds of network traffic so monitoring tools can tell them apart.

subtitle: Identifying IPv6 and MPLS traffic in network monitoring tools.

tldr.problem: Network monitoring tools use RMON (Remote Network Monitoring) to describe and categorize network traffic. Existing RMON protocol identifiers covered IPv4 and older protocols, but not IPv6 or MPLS, making it impossible for monitoring agents to correctly identify and report these newer protocols.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC extends RMON protocol identifier specifications to include IPv6 and MPLS, defining both unicast and multicast MPLS identifiers, and providing encodings for IPv6 and IPv6-in-IPv4 tunneling.
tldr.outcome: Network monitoring tools can now unambiguously identify IPv6 and MPLS traffic in their protocol capability tables, improving interoperability between monitoring agents.

today: RFC 3919 remains an Informational document and has not been obsoleted. Network monitoring tools continue to use these protocol identifiers to recognize and report IPv6 and MPLS traffic.

sections.title: Protocol Identifiers in Network Monitoring
sections.content:
RMON is a management framework that allows network monitoring tools to observe and report on network traffic. A key part of RMON is the protocolDirTable, which lists the network protocols present on a monitored link and describes their relationships. For example, an entry in this table might identify Ethernet frames carrying IP, and a child entry might identify UDP packets inside those IP packets.

RFC 2896 defined protocol identifier macros for many common protocols using the syntax defined in RFC 2895. However, those definitions covered IPv4 and older technologies but not IPv6 or MPLS, which have become increasingly important. RFC 3919 extends these definitions to include IPv6, IPv6-in-IPv4 tunneling, and MPLS (both unicast and multicast variants).

These protocol identifiers are not required to implement RMON-2: a compliant monitoring tool could function without them. However, providing these identifiers improves interoperability and clarity, allowing different monitoring tools to report on the same traffic in consistent ways.
sections.plainLanguage: Network monitors need to say: I see Ethernet carrying IPv6 with UDP inside. Before this memo, they had no standard way to describe IPv6 and MPLS. Now they do.

sections.title: How Protocol Identifiers Work
sections.content:
A protocol identifier is a description of a protocol layer and its parameters. Each identifier defines a CHILDREN property, describing which protocol types can appear inside it. For example, the identifier for Ethernet defines children including IPv4, IPv6, and MPLS. Each child protocol inherits the structure and is indexed according to standardized tables.

Protocol identifiers also define an ADDRESS-FORMAT, specifying how addresses in that protocol layer are represented when monitoring tools report on traffic flows. For IPv6, addresses are 16 octets, stored in network byte order. The source and destination address appear in each IPv6 packet.

Identifiers define a DECODING section that explains how the protocol is recognized in practice. For example, an IPv6 packet over Ethernet is identified by the EtherType 0x86DD. When IPv6 is tunneled inside IPv4 (protocol number 41), monitoring tools must treat the tunnel as a distinct protocol layer.
sections.plainLanguage: Each protocol is like a labeled box: the label says what it is, what can fit inside it, and how to tell it apart from other boxes.

sections.title: IPv6 Protocol Identifiers
sections.content:
The ip6 protocol identifier covers the Internet Protocol Version 6 as defined in RFC 2460. IPv6 packets can be carried over Ethernet (EtherType 0x86DD), over 802.1Q VLAN frames (also 0x86DD), and over MPLS (protocol number 41). The identifier's CHILDREN are determined by the value in the IPv6 Next Header field, which points to the protocol type of the payload (such as 58 for ICMPv6).

Addresses in IPv6 are 16 octets, comprising a source address and a destination address. Monitoring tools use these addresses to identify communication flows between hosts.

The RFC also defines ipip6, the protocol identifier for IPv6 packets tunneled inside IPv4 packets. This is a transitional mechanism that allows IPv6 hosts to communicate over IPv4-only networks. IPv6-in-IPv4 appears as IPv4 protocol number 41. When encapsulated in IPv4, the IPv6 payload retains its own addressing and protocol identification, so monitoring tools must treat the tunnel as a distinct protocol layer.

The RFC defines icmp6 as a child of both ip6 and ipip6, pointing to protocol number 58 (ICMPv6, the control protocol for IPv6).
sections.plainLanguage: IPv6 is a new address system with 16-byte addresses. It can ride inside Ethernet, 802.1Q, or MPLS. When IPv6 is hidden inside IPv4 (tunneling), monitors see a separate layer and must decode both layers.

sections.title: MPLS Protocol Identifiers
sections.content:
MPLS is a forwarding mechanism that simplifies how packets move through networks. Instead of examining destination IP addresses at each router, MPLS routers read short labels and forward packets accordingly. This allows faster forwarding and enables traffic engineering.

MPLS packets are identified by an EtherType value (0x8847 for unicast, 0x8848 for multicast) when carried over Ethernet or 802.1Q. Over PPP links, MPLS uses protocol numbers 0x0281 (unicast) and 0x0283 (multicast).

The RFC defines two protocol identifiers: mplsu for MPLS Unicast and mplsm for MPLS Multicast. Both are references to RFC 3032 (MPLS Label Stack Encoding) and cover the same protocol but with different forwarding models.

A key limitation is that children of MPLS are not systematically identifiable. Because MPLS labels can hide various protocol types, monitoring tools cannot automatically determine what protocol type carries the traffic inside an MPLS label without special configuration or knowledge of how the label is used in a particular network.
sections.plainLanguage: MPLS is like a subway token: instead of checking the destination, the clerk just looks at the token number and sends you to the right train. MPLS tokens can carry IPv4, IPv6, or anything else, but the monitor cannot always tell what is inside.

sections.title: Use in Monitoring and Management
sections.content:
Network monitoring tools use these protocol identifiers to populate the RMON protocolDirTable. When an agent scans a monitored link, it discovers which protocols are present and reports them using these identifiers. A monitoring station can then query the table to understand the protocol stack: for example, discovering that Ethernet carries both IPv4 and IPv6, and that IPv6 appears both natively and tunneled inside IPv4.

These identifiers enable RMON-2 agents to classify traffic flows by protocol layer, count packets and bytes by protocol type, and create filters for monitoring specific protocol combinations. For example, a monitoring tool might report how many IPv6 ICMPv6 packets were exchanged between two hosts, or how many MPLS-labeled packets are being forwarded.

The protocol identifiers follow the established RMON framework defined in RFC 2895 and RFC 2896, ensuring compatibility with existing monitoring tools and management stations. Tools that already implement RMON-2 can adopt these identifiers without architectural changes.
sections.plainLanguage: When you set up a network monitor, it builds a catalog of what it sees on the wire. With these definitions, it can now catalog IPv6 and MPLS traffic the same way it catalogs IPv4.
